transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood), Sarah Patel (Acorn Head of ML), Tom Briggs (Acorn Infra), Jasmine Lee (Acorn Data Sci), Oliver Grant (CTO)
Recording id: ff-20260508-acorn-001

Summary: quick technical deep dive focused on embedding vector dimensionality tradeoffs, batching strategies, KV cache hit behavior, and quantization accuracy vs throughput for a planned on-prem/VPC pilot. Customer wants p95 latency target of <=120ms for rerank path with throughput ~120 req/s. Discussed dedicated vs hosted fallbacks, encryption/KMS, and pilot next steps.

Topics:
- Vector dims: 128 / 256 / 512 tradeoffs
- Batch sizes and continuous batching (b=8,16,32,64)
- KV cache hit-rate expectations and warmup strategies
- Quantization (int8 / fp16 / 4-bit) accuracy regressions
- VPC peering and on-prem container requirements
- Pilot acceptance criteria and benchmarks

Referenced artifacts:
- Pilot bench template: https://redwood.ai/pilot-benchmarks
- Quantization notes (internal): https://redwood.ai/notes/quant-guide (shared after call)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda — vector dims, batching, KV cache, quan — quantization and then on-prem bits. is that right Sarah?
[00:12] Sarah: yep that's perfect, uh we mostly want to know where the cost sweet spot is while keeping quality for our reranker. p95 is the driver.
[00:18] Diego: great. quick context question: your current rerank pipeline — you're doing embedding-based candidate generation then a neural reranker, right?
[00:24] Jasmine: yeah, we do a FAISS ANN for coarse then a neural re-ranker on top. the reranker is currently a 512-d embedding model we trained.
[00:33] Tom: infra wise we're in GCP, but for compliance we'd prefer VPC peering to a Redwood private deployment or an on-prem option later.
[00:40] Priya: cool — that maps to Redwood Private / Dedicated options. for the perf talk we'll assume VPC with private peering unless you say otherwise.
[00:47] Maya: first question: what is your target latency and throughput? you said p95 <=120ms, what about qps?
[00:54] Oliver: we're planning for 100-150 qps steady with spikes up to 300 for peak alerts.
[00:58] Diego: ok expecting 150 sustained. from our benches, a 512-d quantized int8 reranker with batching b=16 on an A10-ish GPU gives p95 ~90-130ms depending on KV cache hit.
[01:12] Sarah: wait — you said 512 quant int8 — what's the accuracy drop vs fp16?
[01:18] Diego: typical drop is 0.5-2% in rerank NDCG for many models, but it depends on your headroom. for medical text sometimes it's closer to the high end. we'll need to run on your holdout.
[01:28] Jasmine: that could be material for us. what's the trade if we move to 256-d?
[01:32] Priya: 256-d gives about 2-3x throughput improvement and roughly half the tokens in KV cache footprint. accuracy loss varies — for some rerank models it's 1-4% relative, but again depends on training.
[01:44] Tom: also curious about memory. what's the KV cache memory savings between 512 and 256?
[01:49] Diego: ballpark: KV size scales linearly with vector dim. so 512->256 halves KV bytes. on a 40 GB GPU, you can host roughly XK tokens — but depends on sequence length. our runtime can spill to host RAM for very large contexts but that costs latency.
[02:05] Sarah: can you explain the KV cache warmup behavior? we have long-tail queries and cold starts are a concern.
[02:12] Diego: sure. two parts: prefix caching for repeated beginnings and full KV reuse for rerank candidate prompts. we've seen hit-rates climb to 60-80% after steady-state for common prefixes. for truly ad-hoc queries hit is lower. we recommend a hybrid: short warmup period and a small LRU cache pre-seeded with common contexts.
[02:28] Oliver: hmm how do you pre-seed? is that manual?
[02:31] Priya: you can provide typical prompts or we can bootstrap from logs. in Dedicated/Private we have APIs to upload pre-seed entries.
[02:37] Tom: about batching — our latency SLO is strict. how aggressive can we batch before p95 blows past 120ms?
[02:44] Diego: it depends on arrival distribution. synchronous batching b=32 gave p95 in our lab ~180ms at 150 qps on a mid-tier GPU. continuous batching with adaptive time windows (we call it micro-batching) can get you the throughput of b=32 while keeping tail latency near b=8 numbers, but that requires the runtime to be tuned — which Redwood does by default in Dedicated.
[03:04] Sarah: can you quantify cost differences? we want per-request CPU/GPU cost numbers.
[03:09] Maya: yes, we'll share a cost model. rough numbers: 512 fp16 at b=8 ~ $Y per 1k requests, 512 int8 at b=16 is about 30-40% cheaper per request. moving to 256 dims roughly halves embedding compute cost in the generator stage and reduces rerank cost by ~45% in practice.
[03:26] Jasmine: are there accuracy benchmarks where lower dim actually helps due to less overfitting?
[03:31] Diego: interesting — sometimes smaller dims regularize poorly trained heads and can help generalization, but it's case dependent. we'll test on your dataset.
[03:38] Tom: for on-prem — what are the packaging requirements? containers? bare-metal?
[03:42] Priya: for Private on-prem we provide an OCI bundle and helm charts; typical install needs GPU drivers, our runtime, and a control-plane agent. KMS integration is via your HSM or cloud KMS. networking needs: egress for control plane or fully air-gapped with an offline license.
[03:58] Oliver: encryption at rest — can we use our Vault/HSM?
[04:01] Maya: yes we support external KMS/HSM with customer-managed keys. that's in the SOC2 docs I'll send.
[04:06] Sarah: about model fallbacks — if dedicated capacity is saturated do you automatically route to hosted variants? we need deterministic SLA behavior.
[04:12] Diego: yes route policies can prefer Dedicated and failover to hosted or lower-capacity model variants. you can set cost-based or latency-based policies. fallback may incur different privacy guarantees — we'll note that in T&Cs.
[04:24] Jasmine: quick question on quant 4-bit — is that realistic for rerank?
[04:28] Diego: 4-bit can be hit-or-miss. we can do 4-bit PTQ with minimal retraining but expect more accuracy variance. for non-critical applications it's great for cost; for medical rerank I usually recommend int8 or mixed int8+fp16 for sensitive layers.
[04:44] Sarah: what about vector dims for embeddings used in vector DB? that's upstream of rerank — we don't want to re-run expensive indexing every time we change dims.
[04:51] Maya: good point. you can keep ANN index at higher dims and do dimensionality reduction on-the-fly for candidate generation, or precompute alternate indices for A/B tests. part of pilot is to measure reindex costs.
[05:03] Tom: can Redwood run initial microbench on our cloud infra with an image?
[05:07] Diego: yes, we can run a three-day microbench using a dedicated instance in your project via a temporary service account. we'll need billing/permissions and an S3/GCS path with sample vectors.
[05:17] Oliver: timeline wise we want results within two weeks.
[05:20] Maya: we'll aim for that. Diego will run benches; Sarah will upload samples.
[05:24] (crosstalk)
[05:26] Jasmine: small nit — you mentioned p50 numbers before, what's realistic?
[05:29] Diego: p50 for 512 int8 with b=16 was ~40-60ms in our test. p95 is the harder metric.
[05:35] Sarah: how about tail latency mitigation options beyond batching?
[05:38] Priya: we use warm lanes for high-priority requests (dedicated cold-avoid pools), fast-path quant kernels, and prefetching of KV entries for predicted prompts. also per-route SLAs and token budgeting in the runtime.
[05:51] Tom: any limitations for quant on newer transformer layers we use? we have some custom attention variants.
[05:57] Diego: custom kernels may need a compatibility pass. our runtime has a plugin interface and we can onboard custom ops, but that adds integration work. we'd want a quick compat scan during pilot.
[06:08] Sarah: what exact metrics will you produce in the bench report?
[06:11] Diego: p50/p90/p95 latencies, throughput qps, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rates over time, memory footprint, and accuracy delta vs your baseline. CSV + annotated plots.
[06:22] Maya: action recap: Diego runs microbench, Sarah uploads data, Maya shares security/shopper docs and cost model.
[06:29] Oliver: one more legal Q — does pilot data get deleted after tests?
[06:33] Maya: yes — we have a data-retention clause and can delete artifacts on customer request; will include steps in pilot T&Cs.
[06:40] Sarah: perfect. thanks everyone.
[06:42] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up with links and schedule.
[06:45] [END]
